Each node operates independently, exchanging messages through a shared medium—abstracted here as a digital data communication network. This setup enables modular decomposition of complex systems into manageable components. The relationship between client and server emerges from the execution context of their respective programs, implying a dual role: one acts as requester, the other as responder. These roles are not fixed but emerge from programmatic behavior rather than static configuration. The system's robustness depends on its ability to maintain consistent message flow despite potential delays or failures in transmission. In GSI, this translates to Bayesian inference over client-side queries and server-side relevance scoring, where uncertainty is propagated through probabilistic kernels. In GSE, it manifests as a state machine transitioning between local and remote execution states, adapting to environmental changes in real-time. The modularity inherent in network topology allows for scalable expansion while preserving functional coherence. This principle underpins both the theoretical and practical frameworks of distributed computing and intelligent search systems.
